strengths: The paper unifies latent chain-of-thought reasoning (Coconut-style hidden-state generation) with cross-agent latent communication via KV-cache transfer into a single end-to-end, training-free framework (LatentMAS), which is a natural but previously unexplored combination in the MAS literature.

The evaluation is broad: 9 benchmarks spanning math/science reasoning, commonsense, and code generation, across 3 model scales (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B) and 2 MAS architectures (sequential and hierarchical), with three metrics (accuracy, token usage, end-to-end speed) and baselines accelerated with vLLM, which strengthens the fairness of the efficiency comparisons.
Efficiency gains are substantial and well-documented: 70-84% fewer output tokens and 2.6x-7x speed-up over text-based MAS, which is practically valuable for deployment.

Useful ablations: the input-output alignment matrix W_a is validated both qualitatively (embedding-space drift analysis, Figure 6) and quantitatively (2.3-5.3% accuracy gains, Figure 7), and the latent-step-depth sweep (Figure 8) provides practical guidance on the m hyperparameter.

The method is simple, training-free, and implementable with standard HuggingFace/vLLM interfaces, which aids reproducibility and practical adoption; prompt templates and evaluation protocols are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited novelty beyond composition: the two core ingredients (auto-regressive latent thought generation and cross-model KV-cache exchange) closely follow Coconut (Hao et al., 2024) and Cache-to-Cache/KVComm (Fu et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025). The main new technical component is the alignment matrix W_a computed as a ridge-regression pseudo-inverse of W_out, which is a straightforward heuristic.

The theoretical contributions are weak or circular. Theorem 3.1 rests on a highly idealized Linear Representation Hypothesis with ternary coefficients and yields only a counting argument; Theorem 3.3 (lossless information preservation) is essentially a restatement of how KV caches work when the same model processes the same inputs; Theorem A.1 bounds the Wasserstein distance by the very quantity that W_a minimizes, so the 'justification' is circular. The complexity comparison in Theorem 3.4 inherits the questionable m' = O(d_h*m/log|V|) assumption.

The framework critically assumes homogeneous agents (same architecture, hidden size, layer count) for KV-cache transfer; heterogeneous agents are deferred to a two-sentence mention with no experiments. This substantially limits generality of 'latent collaboration' and makes the multi-agent setting somewhat artificial (all agents are copies of the same model).

Accuracy gains over the text-based MAS baseline are modest and inconsistent: on average only 2.8-4.6% over TextMAS, with several negative results (GSM8K sequential 8B -1.9, ARC-E hierarchical -0.3, ARC-C -0.2, AIME25 hierarchical 0.0). On small benchmarks like AIME (30 problems), a 3.3-point gain equals a single problem. The headline 'up to 14.6%' is measured against the weaker single-model baseline. No statistical significance tests or variance estimates are reported despite averaging 3 runs.

The central claim of 'lossless' communication is only meaningful because agents share the same representation space; no analysis is given of how errors or distributional drift compound across longer agent chains, and the semantic analysis (Figure 5) is qualitative 2D scatter plots with an unspecified projection.

The latent-step-depth ablation (Figure 8) covers only easy tasks (ARC, GSM8K), and the choice of m per task/how it interacts with harder benchmarks (AIME, GPQA) is not analyzed. No code release is mentioned, which, combined with the engineering-heavy method, weakens reproducibility.

Limitations discussion is thin: beyond the heterogeneous-agent remark, there is no discussion of failure modes (e.g., when latent thoughts diverge from text semantics), interpretability costs of fully latent collaboration, or sensitivity to the alignment matrix on out-of-distribution inputs.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and interesting question: whether multi-agent LLM collaboration can be performed entirely in latent space rather than through text, unifying latent CoT-style reasoning (Coconut-style) with cross-agent KV-cache transfer.

The framework is training-free and empirically evaluated at scale: 9 benchmarks, two MAS architectures, and three Qwen3 model scales (4B/8B/14B), with three metrics (accuracy, token usage, end-to-end speed) and vLLM-accelerated baselines, which is a fairly comprehensive experimental grid.

The ridge-regression alignment operator W_a for mapping last-layer hidden states back to the input embedding space is a sensible, cheap engineering solution, and the paper provides both a theoretical bound (Theorem A.1) and ablations (Figures 6-7) supporting it.

The paper is generally well-organized, with clear notation, a roadmap, ablations on latent step depth, and a reasonably detailed appendix including prompts (Appendix E), which aids reproducibility of the setup.
weaknesses: The central 'losslessness' claim is overclaimed and nearly tautological. Theorem 3.3 shows KV-cache transfer is equivalent to re-feeding the same model's outputs as context - this only holds because all agents share identical architecture and weights (same Qwen3 model). What is presented as a deep property of 'latent collaboration' is essentially the observation that a single model with a longer context is equivalent to itself. This also means the system is arguably not a genuine multi-agent system over distinct models, a limitation only briefly acknowledged in Appendix C.3, where the proposed fix (trainable adapters) contradicts the 'training-free' claim.

The expressiveness theory rests on an unrealistically strong assumption. Theorem 3.1's Linear Representation Hypothesis (ternary {0,+1,-1} coefficients over an independent semantic basis, Assumption B.1) is a counting argument over an idealized embedding space, not a statement about actual LLM representations. The derived '235.7x/377.1x more efficient' numbers and the complexity comparison in Theorem 3.4 therefore quantify a gap between a hypothetical latent system and an equally hypothetical text system, not between LatentMAS and real TextMAS; presenting these as evidence of practical advantage is misleading.

Baseline fairness and metric comparability are questionable. LatentMAS agents produce m latent steps that are never decoded, so 'token usage' is inherently near zero for intermediate agents, making the 70-84% token reduction largely a definitional artifact rather than a measured efficiency gain. Accuracy gains over TextMAS are modest (2.8%/4.6% on average, with several tasks showing ~0 to +0.3, and some negative, e.g., GSM8K hierarchical 8B), while 'up to 14.6%' headlines the comparison against the weaker single-model baseline.

Statistical rigor is insufficient for the small benchmarks used. AIME24/25 contain 30 problems each, so reported gains of 3.3 points correspond to a single problem; three runs are averaged but no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported anywhere.

There is an apparent inconsistency in the method/prompt design that undermines confidence in the implementation: the Critic agent's prompt instructs it to output '(1) original plan contents (Copy the provided Planner Agent's plan here)' even though the Critic receives the plan only as latent KV representation and cannot decode it to text. Either the design description or the prompts are inconsistent, and this is never explained.

Supporting analyses are weak. Figure 5's claim that latent thoughts are 'more expressive' is based on visual inspection of 2D projections of embedding dimensions 1 and 2 over one dataset (MedQA); the case study in Appendix D is a single cherry-picked GSM8K example. No analysis addresses error propagation, failure modes, or when latent collaboration degrades.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, hyperparameters were tuned (with the tuning protocol not described), and the framework is restricted to homogeneous same-family models, limiting independent verification and generalization.

Novelty is moderate: the work is primarily a combination of existing ingredients - Coconut-style hidden-state auto-regression (Hao et al., 2024), KV-cache-based cross-model communication (Fu et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2024) - assembled into a pipeline without new learning or a fundamentally new mechanism, and the paper's own related work makes this proximity clear.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and well-motivated question — replacing text-mediated communication in LLM multi-agent systems with direct latent-space collaboration — and the proposed mechanism (auto-regressive last-layer hidden-state generation plus layer-wise KV-cache 'working memory' transfer) is clean, training-free, and clearly described.

The evaluation is broad: 9 benchmarks across math/science, commonsense, and code generation, two MAS architectures, and three backbone scales (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B), with three metrics (accuracy, tokens, end-to-end speed) and vLLM-accelerated baselines, which strengthens the efficiency claims.

The ablations are targeted and useful: the input-output alignment matrix W_a is validated both distributionally (Figure 6) and via downstream accuracy (Figure 7, +2.3%-5.3%), and the latent-step-depth analysis (Figure 8) gives practical guidance on the accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

The alignment operator is a practical contribution in itself: a closed-form ridge-regression solution computed once and reused, with an accompanying Wasserstein upper-bound analysis (Theorem A.1) that justifies the design.

The prompt templates (Appendix E), evaluation protocols, and implementation details (HF past_key_values, ridge formulation of W_a) are reported at a level of detail that supports reproducibility of the core method.
weaknesses: The 'multi-agent' framing is weaker than claimed: all experiments use a single model family playing multiple prompted roles. The KV-cache transfer trivially works only because all agents share identical weights and layer shapes; heterogeneous agents are deferred to a two-sentence appendix discussion requiring a trainable adapter. The system is thus closer to latent/continuous CoT with KV sharing across prompts of one model than to genuine multi-model collaboration, and this central limitation is not acknowledged as such in the main text.

The headline theoretical results are loose and arguably oversold. Theorem 3.1 rests on an artificial Linear Representation Hypothesis with ternary {0,+1,-1} coefficients and a counting argument; the derived '235x/377x/471x more efficient' figures follow mechanically from this assumption but are not empirically corroborated (measured speedup is ~4x, two orders of magnitude smaller). Theorem 3.3 is essentially the standard observation that reusing a KV cache equals recomputing it, presented as a novel 'lossless transfer' guarantee.

Missing empirical comparison with the closest related work. Cache-to-Cache (Fu et al., 2025), KVComm (Ye et al., 2025a), and Thought Communication (Zheng et al., 2025) are cited as closely related latent/KV communication methods but are not run as baselines, so the claimed superiority of the working-memory transfer design over prior cache-sharing approaches is not directly evidenced.

Statistical rigor is thin given the magnitude of some claims. Results are means over 3 runs with no variance or significance tests; on 30-problem benchmarks (AIME24/25), gains of +3.3-3.4 points correspond to roughly one problem and may be noise. Several cells also show LatentMAS underperforming TextMAS (e.g., ARC-E/GSM8K in Table 1 and Table 2), which complicates the 'consistently outperforms' narrative and is not analyzed.

The latent step budget m is tuned over {0,10,20,40,80} per task, so 'training-free' understates the per-task tuning burden; the sensitivity of results to this choice on the reasoning benchmarks (where the headline gains are largest) is not reported.

There is no explicit limitations section, no code release statement, and the interpretability/failure-mode implications of communicating in latent space (agents cannot inspect what they receive, evidenced by the 'the latent information might contain irrelevant contents' prompt patches) are not discussed.

Some evidence is qualitative and weakly indicative: Figure 5's 2D embedding scatter plots are used to claim 'greater diversity and expressive capacity' of latent thoughts, which over-interpret projection plots, and the single GSM8K case study cannot support the general claim about error-compounding mitigation.
